title: Dear Diary...
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and practice of diaries and journaling, from ancient logbooks and Japanese pillow books in tenth-century Japan through Renaissance individualism, nineteenth-century published diaries, and blogging. They profile famous diarists (Samuel Pepys, Michael Shiner, Josie Underwood, Robert Falcon Scott, Anaïs Nin, Anne Frank), then cover therapeutic expressive writing (James Pennebaker, Ira Progoff's intensive journaling), gratitude journals, morning pages, bullet journals, and dream journals. The episode ends with a listener mail from Evan Whitby about movie and show recommendations.

entities.name: The Diary of a Young Girl

segments.title: Tour promo
segments.summary: Hosts promote upcoming live tour dates in Orlando, Atlanta, and Nashville with ticket info.

segments.title: Opening banter on keeping journals
segments.summary: Hosts ask whether they have kept diaries; Josh describes his friend Mike Anderson's daily journal kept since 1991.

segments.title: Early records and pillow books
segments.summary: Early non-diary records such as an Egyptian official's logbook and Marcus Aurelius's Meditations are distinguished from true diaries. Tenth-century Japanese court women's pillow books are presented as the first diaries, written in hiragana.

segments.title: Pillow books, The Tale of Genji, and the Pillow Book film
segments.summary: Pillow books mixed court events, gossip, fiction and poetry. The Tale of Genji by Murasaki Shikibu is described as growing out of this tradition. Josh mentions Sei Shonagon's Pillow Book and the 1996 Peter Greenaway film.

segments.title: Journaling in the Renaissance, Puritans, and French and British intimate journals
segments.summary: Journaling spread with Renaissance individualism. Puritans and Quakers kept religiously focused diaries, the French developed the intimate journal during the Revolution, and the British followed in the early nineteenth century. Publishing old diaries became a new literary form.

segments.title: Published diaries and blogging
segments.summary: Publishing private journals raised questions about writing for oneself versus an audience. Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest is cited. Blogging in the late nineties let people share diaries privately or anonymously, leading to social media.

segments.title: Transition to famous diaries
segments.summary: Hosts take a break and introduce a discussion of famous historical diaries.

segments.title: Samuel Pepys
segments.summary: Samuel Pepys's nine-year shorthand diary covers the Restoration, the Great Plague and Great Fire of London, his marriage, and his new watch. Chuck notes his diary runs over a million words, comparable to the Harry Potter series.

segments.title: Michael Shiner and Josie Underwood
segments.summary: Michael Shiner, a formerly enslaved man who worked at the Washington Naval Yard, kept a 56-year diary, self-taught with unconventional spelling and punctuation. Josie Underwood's Civil War diary from a Kentucky slaveholding family in Bowling Green, sympathetic to the Union, is described as a famous civilian account, mixing war events with society life.

segments.title: Robert Falcon Scott's expedition journal
segments.summary: Captain Robert Falcon Scott's journal chronicles the 1912 South Pole expedition, which arrived a month after a rival and then died trying to return.

segments.title: Anaïs Nin and Anne Frank
segments.summary: Anaïs Nin's diary, begun at age eleven in 1914, was published in a sanitized form in 1966 and she later published more openly, becoming a feminist icon. Anne Frank's diary, written 1942 to 1944 while hiding from the Nazis, was rewritten for publication; her father Otto published the version after the war. Hosts mention visiting the Anne Frank House.

segments.title: Transition to why people journal
segments.summary: Hosts take a break and set up a discussion of why people write journals.

segments.title: Therapeutic journaling and expressive writing
segments.summary: Therapist Ira Progoff developed intensive journaling in the 1960s. James Pennebaker's expressive writing research found short sessions writing about trauma can relieve psychological and physical symptoms, with a short-term rise in distress; hosts note the risks of journaling too soon after trauma and advise therapist involvement.

segments.title: Gratitude journals and self-distancing
segments.summary: Gratitude journaling is discussed, including a 2021 meta-analysis by Japanese researchers finding benefits for stress and depression, and advice to focus on single people-focused entries. A 2016 study by G. Jung Park found expressive journaling increases self-distancing.

segments.title: Private truth and journaling habits
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the idea of the truth one tells oneself in a private journal, the caution that journaling daily may increase rumination, and that journaling is not a requirement. Josh recounts a quarter-long commonplace journal from a playwriting class in college that he lost.

segments.title: Morning pages, bullet journals
segments.summary: Julia Cameron's The Artist's Way recommends morning pages, a stream-of-consciousness writing practice; hosts note the claimed Jungian basis is dubious. Bullet journals, created by digital designer Ryder Carroll in 2013, are described as life-organizing systems for to-do lists, calendars, and goals.

segments.title: Dream journals
segments.summary: Dream journals record dreams before they fade; a New York Times letter describes how logging dreams changed how the writer saw people in waking life. Hosts discuss carrying dream emotions into waking life.

segments.title: Anecdote about actor sighting and TV show mix-up
segments.summary: Hosts swap personal anecdotes: Chuck describes lingering TV tension into commercial breaks, and Josh recounts meeting an actor from The Killing in New York, with a back-and-forth about the cast and names.

segments.title: Listener mail from Evan Whitby
segments.summary: Evan Whitby of Hendersonville, North Carolina thanks the show for movie and TV recommendations, including What We Do in the Shadows, Reservation Dogs, The Larry Sanders Show, Nate Bargatze's stand-up, Eyes Wide Shut, and Dick Town.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener mail at the show's email address and close with credits.
